title: Clinical psychology
description: Branch of medicine focused on mental disorders
wiki_lead:
Clinical psychology is an integration of human science, behavioral science, theory, and clinical knowledge aimed at understanding, preventing, and relieving psychological distress or dysfunction as well as promoting  well-being and personal growth. Central to its practice are psychological assessment, diagnosis, clinical formulation, and psychotherapy; although clinical psychologists also engage in research, teaching, consultation, forensic testimony, and program development and administration. In many countries, clinical psychology is a regulated mental health profession. In the United States, clinical psychologists operate under the same license as counseling psychologists and school psychologists.
The field is generally considered to have begun in 1896 with the opening of the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania by Lightner Witmer. In the first half of the 20th century, clinical psychology was focused on psychological assessment, with little attention given to treatment. This changed after the 1940s when World War II resulted in the need for a large increase in the number of trained clinicians. Since that time, three main educational models have developed in the US—the PhD Clinical Science model (heavily focused on research), the PhD science-practitioner model (integrating scientific research and practice), and the PsyD practitioner-scholar model (focusing on clinical theory and practice). In the UK and Ireland, the Clinical Psychology Doctorate falls between the latter two of these models, whilst in much of mainland Europe, the training is at the master's level and predominantly psychotherapist. Clinical psychologists are expert in providing psychotherapy, and generally train within four primary theoretical orientations—psychodynamic, humanistic, cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), and systems or family therapy.
Clinical psychology is different from psychiatry. Although practitioners in both fields are experts in mental health, clinical psychologists are experts in psychological assessment, including neuropsychological and psychometric assessment, and they treat mental disorders primarily through psychotherapy. Currently, there are nine US states (Louisiana, New Mexico, Illinois, Iowa, Idaho, Colorado, Utah, Vermont, and, most recently, Hawaii) which allow clinical psychologists with advanced specialty training to prescribe psychotropic medications. Psychiatrists are medical doctors who specialize in the treatment of mental disorders via a variety of methods, including diagnostic assessment, psychotherapy, psychoactive medications, and medical procedures such as electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) or transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). Psychiatrists do not as standard have advanced training in psychometrics or psychotherapy equivalent to that of Clinical Psychologists.

History

The earliest recorded approaches to assess and treat mental distress were a combination of religious, magical, or medical perspectives. In the early 19th century, one approach to study mental conditions and behavior was using phrenology, the study of personality by examining the shape of the skull. Other popular treatments at that time included the study of the shape of the face (physiognomy) and Mesmer's treatment for mental conditions using magnets (mesmerism). Spiritualism and Phineas Quimby's "mental healing" were also popular.
While the scientific community eventually came to reject all of these methods for treating mental illness, academic psychologists also were not concerned with serious forms of mental illness. The study of mental illness was already being done in the developing fields of psychiatry and neurology within the asylum movement. It was not until the end of the 19th century, around the time when Sigmund Freud was first developing his "talking cure" in Vienna, that the first scientific application of clinical psychology began.

grok_lead: Clinical psychology is the branch of psychology that specializes in the research, assessment, diagnosis, evaluation, prevention, and treatment of emotional and behavioral disorders. It focuses on providing continuing and comprehensive mental and behavioral health care for individuals, families, and groups, integrating the science of psychology to address complex human problems and promote positive change. Clinical psychologists apply evidence-based methods to understand, prevent, and alleviate psychological distress, drawing on empirical research to inform interventions that enhance well-being and resilience. The field traces its origins to the late 19th century in the United States, with Lightner Witmer establishing the first psychological clinic in 1896 at the University of Pennsylvania, where he coined the term "clinical psychology" to describe the application of psychological principles to practical problems in education and adjustment. Early developments were influenced by the psychometric tradition, emphasizing assessment tools like intelligence tests, and grew significantly after World War I due to the need for evaluating and treating veterans with psychological issues. The profession formalized in the mid-20th century, particularly following World War II, when the Boulder Conference in 1949 established the scientist-practitioner model, integrating research and clinical practice as core training components. This model remains foundational, though contemporary approaches also include the practitioner-scholar model emphasized in PsyD programs. Clinical psychologists work in diverse settings, including hospitals, private practices, schools, and research institutions, where they conduct psychological assessments using standardized tests and interviews to diagnose conditions such as anxiety, depression, and schizophrenia. Treatment often involves psychotherapy modalities like cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) or psychodynamic approaches, tailored to individual needs and supported by ongoing outcome research. They also engage in prevention efforts, such as community programs to reduce stigma around mental health, and collaborate with other healthcare professionals to address biopsychosocial factors in disorders. The scope extends to specialized areas like clinical child psychology, which applies scientific knowledge to developmental and family issues, and clinical health psychology, focusing on psychological aspects of physical illness. Training to become a clinical psychologist typically requires a doctoral degree, either a PhD in psychology, which emphasizes research, or a PsyD, which prioritizes clinical practice, followed by a one-year internship and postdoctoral supervision. Programs accredited by the American Psychological Association (APA) ensure rigorous standards, including coursework in psychopathology, ethics, and statistics, as well as supervised clinical hours exceeding 2,000. Licensure varies by jurisdiction but generally demands passing the Examination for Professional Practice in Psychology (EPPP) and accumulating additional supervised experience. With mental health needs rising globally, clinical psychology continues to evolve, incorporating advances in neuroscience, telehealth, AI-driven tools, and culturally sensitive practices to meet diverse populations' demands.
